text: The Bust of Charles I was a sculptural work created by the Italian artist Gianlorenzo Bernini, which one historian described as "setting the visual conventions for centuries... [establishing itself as] the official portrait of secular absolutism." The sculpture depicted King Charles I of England, who wrote to Bernini praising the artist's name as "exalted above those of all men of talent who have exercised your profession." Bernini never traveled to London to complete the bust; instead, he used a painted triple portrait of Charles I, created by the Flemish artist Anthony van Dyck, specifically for this purpose. Although Bernini never met Charles I in person, the bust was regarded as a success at the time, and Charles rewarded Bernini with jewelry valued at over 4,000 Roman scudi—more than 60 times the average yearly salary of a worker in Rome. Pope Urban VIII sent the bust to Charles's queen, Henrietta Maria, in 1637, in an effort to promote reconciliation between the Roman Catholic Church and the Church of England. The bust was presented in 1637 and was admired for its craftsmanship and resemblance to the king. Charles also gave Bernini a valuable diamond ring. Henrietta Maria commissioned a companion bust of herself, but the English Civil War prevented its completion. After the English Civil War, the bust was sold but was later recovered and added to the Royal Collection during the Restoration, only to be destroyed by a fire at Whitehall Palace in January 1698. Numerous copies of the bust exist in various forms, including engravings and bronze sculptures. For a period in the 19th and early 20th centuries, there was a belief in England and elsewhere that Bernini had also produced a bust of Oliver Cromwell, the victor over Charles I in the English Civil War; however, this attribution was refuted in 1922.
